column3: Says Joseph “took his two sons with him,” rather than describing him as setting out with them.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
“An assembly of peoples” retains the assembly term rendered “a multitude of peoples.”
“They are mine” is a direct statement rather than “shall be reckoned as mine.”
Describes the offspring as those “you fathered,” using an active verb rather than “children born to you.”
“Rachel died upon me” retains the personal expression rendered “to my sorrow Rachel died.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Retains “my sons” and the unnamed “he said,” rather than identifying the second speaker as Jacob.
The eyes are “heavy” from age, and Israel “could not see,” rather than “could hardly see.”
Does not explicitly add “again” to seeing Joseph’s face; “your seed” retains the collective image rendered “your children.”
Retains “his knees,” without explicitly naming his father, and the direction “to the earth.”
Close to the Hebrew.
“For Manasseh was the firstborn” preserves the causal wording rather than “although.”
Close to the Hebrew.
“May my name be called in them” retains the name as the grammatical subject, rather than making the boys the subject of being called.
“It was displeasing in his eyes” retains the image rendered “he was displeased.”
Close to the Hebrew.
“The fullness of the nations” retains the fullness term rather than “a multitude of nations.”
Does not name Jacob again at the beginning of the verse; “By you Israel will bless” precedes the quoted blessing.
Close to the Hebrew.
“One portion above your brothers” keeps the portion as what exceeds their share, rather than describing Joseph himself as “one who is above your brothers.”
